summary: Mobility is returning to near‑normal levels (MF‑Index 71) and fuel prices remain high, curbing travel demand. Public transport ridership is recovering but still below pre‑pandemic levels, while actual fuel savings from work‑from‑home are far below the theoretical ceiling. High‑mobility sectors such as logistics and construction pose economic and environmental risks that need targeted policy attention.

signals.detail: Although the modelled ceiling suggests 35.7 M L/week could be saved, only 0.334 M L were actually saved in the first week of the mandate, indicating very low compliance and limited real‑world fuel‑saving impact.

Daily PT trips reached 1.24 M, reflecting a rebound toward the 2019 level (≈1.43 M daily) and supporting the ridership component of 72.7/100, but further growth is needed to fully restore pre‑pandemic volumes.

Sectors with the highest mobility scores (logistics 92, construction 95, retail 85) remain at high risk of congestion, emissions and supply‑chain strain, offsetting the benefits of higher fuel prices.

Work‑from‑home adoption is uneven: public & GLCs at 60% versus retail (15%), logistics (8%) and construction (5%). This disparity concentrates travel burden on lower‑wage, high‑mobility workers and raises equity concerns.
Elevated fuel prices (RON95 RM4.42/L) create incentives for a shift to public transport, yet PT capacity constraints and modest ridership recovery limit the magnitude of a lasting modal transition.

recommendation: Introduce targeted incentives for remote work in logistics, retail and construction to raise sectoral WFH rates to at least 30% by Q2 2027, and implement a fuel‑efficiency rebate that aims for a verified weekly saving of 2 M L. Simultaneously, expand PT capacity and subsidise fares to lift daily ridership to 1.5 M trips by end‑2027, while monitoring equity impacts across sectors.
